EVPO: Explained Variance Policy Optimization for
Adaptive Critic Utilization in LLM Post-Training

Chengjun Pan ††thanks: Equal contribution. †Corresponding authors:tgui@fudan.edu.cn, fengyansong@pku.edu.cn Affiliation: Peking University    Shichun Liu* Affiliation: Fudan University    Jiahang Lin* Affiliation: Fudan University    Dingwei Zhu Affiliation: Fudan University    Jiazheng Zhang Affiliation: Fudan University    Shihan Dou Affiliation: Fudan University    Songyang Gao Affiliation: Shanghai AI Lab    Zhenhua Han Affiliation: Shanghai Qiji Zhifeng Co., Ltd.    Binghai Wang Affiliation: Fudan University    Rui Zheng Affiliation: Shanghai Qiji Zhifeng Co., Ltd.    Xuanjing Huang Affiliation: Fudan University    Tao Gui† Affiliation: Fudan University    Yansong Feng† Affiliation: Peking University
Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) for LLM post-training faces a fundamental design choice: whether to use a learned critic as a baseline for policy optimization. Classical theory favors critic-based methods such as PPO for variance reduction, yet critic-free alternatives like GRPO have gained widespread adoption due to their simplicity and competitive performance. We show that in sparse-reward settings, a learned critic can inject estimation noise that exceeds the state signal it captures, increasing rather than reducing advantage variance. By casting baseline selection as a Kalman filtering problem, we unify PPO and GRPO as two extremes of the Kalman gain and prove that explained variance (EV), computable from a single training batch, identifies the exact boundary: positive EV indicates the critic reduces variance, while zero or negative EV signals that it inflates variance. Building on this insight, we propose Explained Variance Policy Optimization (EVPO), which monitors batch-level EV at each training step and adaptively switches between critic-based and batch-mean advantage estimation, provably achieving no greater variance than the better of the two at every step. Across four tasks spanning classical control, agentic interaction, and mathematical reasoning, EVPO consistently outperforms both PPO and GRPO regardless of which fixed baseline is stronger on a given task. Further analysis confirms that the adaptive gating tracks critic maturation over training and that the theoretically derived zero threshold is empirically optimal.

1 Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a central paradigm for LLM post-training, driving advances in mathematical reasoning [10, 27, 20, 33], instruction following [37, 6, 8], and interactive decision-making [26, 31, 3]. A prominent instantiation is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) [10], where a sparse reward is assigned only at the terminal step via an automatic verifier. A fundamental algorithmic choice in this setting is whether to employ a critic (a learned value function) as a baseline for policy optimization.

Classical RL theory holds that a critic reduces policy-gradient variance by providing a state-dependent baseline [28, 22], forming the foundation of actor-critic methods including PPO [23]. In practice, however, critic-free methods such as GRPO [25, 10] have gained widespread adoption, as they are cheaper and can match or even surpass PPO [11]. Rather than treating the critic as a binary design choice, we ask:

In sparse-reward LLM post-training, when does a learned critic help and when does it hurt?

To answer this, we identify three progressive sub-questions. 𝒬1\mathcal{Q}_{1}: Is the boundary observable? Critic quality fluctuates during training, and we need to measure its impact on policy optimization in a controlled setting. 𝒬2\mathcal{Q}_{2}: Where exactly is the boundary? In sparse-reward LLM generation, the critic may inject more estimation noise than the state signal it captures. We need a precise characterization of when this happens. 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}: Can this boundary be exploited online? If the helpful-vs-harmful regime can be detected in real time, we can build an algorithm that adapts rather than committing to a fixed choice.

We adopt explained variance (EV), the fraction of return variance accounted for by the critic, as a real-time proxy for critic usefulness. Empirically (𝒬1\mathcal{Q}_{1}), EV remains negative during the early stage of training, and controlled interventions (suppressing the critic or injecting noise) confirm that performance degrades once EV falls to zero or below, suggesting that its sign reliably indicates whether the critic helps or hurts (Section 2.2). To pinpoint the boundary (𝒬2\mathcal{Q}_{2}), we cast baseline selection as a Kalman filtering problem [14] in which the critic and the batch-mean return are two competing estimators of the true state value, with PPO and GRPO corresponding to the two extremes of the Kalman gain (Section 2.3). We prove that the sign of EV, computable from a single batch, is sufficient to determine which extreme is preferable (Theorem 1), placing the boundary at EV=0\text{EV}=0.

Exploiting this boundary online (𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}), we propose Explained Variance Policy Optimization (EVPO), which implements this adaptive hard gating at each training step. EVPO maintains a standard PPO-style critic alongside the policy, and at each iteration computes batch-level EV as a scalar indicator. When EV is positive, the critic captures meaningful state-dependent signal, and EVPO uses its predictions as the baseline (the PPO mode); when EV falls to zero or below, EVPO discards the critic and falls back to the batch-mean return (the GRPO mode). We prove that this switching rule yields advantage-estimator variance no greater than the better of PPO and GRPO at every step, so EVPO never underperforms either fixed choice.

We evaluate EVPO on four tasks spanning classical control, interactive decision-making, and mathematical reasoning. Across all tasks, EVPO achieves the best final performance and maintains its advantage throughout training, regardless of whether PPO or GRPO is the stronger fixed baseline on a given task. Further analysis confirms that the adaptive gating tracks critic maturation over training and that the theoretically motivated zero threshold is empirically optimal.

Our main contributions are:

  1. 1.

    Indicator and theory. We unify PPO and GRPO as two extremes of a Kalman baseline-selection spectrum and prove that the sign of explained variance is the exact boundary separating the variance-reducing from the variance-inflating critic regime (Theorem 1).

  2. 2.

    Algorithm. We propose EVPO, a lightweight method that switches between critic-based and critic-free advantage estimation via batch-level EV, with a provable guarantee of no greater variance than the better of PPO and GRPO at every step.

  3. 3.

    Empirical validation. EVPO consistently outperforms fixed PPO and GRPO across four tasks spanning classical control, agentic interaction, and mathematical reasoning. Analysis experiments confirm that the zero threshold is empirically optimal and that the adaptive gating reflects critic maturation across training stages.

2 Preliminaries

This section establishes that the critic is not uniformly beneficial. We review PPO and GRPO as two baseline-selection extremes (Section 2.1), then show empirically that the sign of explained variance reliably predicts whether the critic helps or hurts (Section 2.2).

2.1 RL for LLM Post-Training

We model autoregressive text generation as a token-level Markov Decision Process [18, 29, 36]. Given a prompt xx, the policy πθ\pi_{\theta} generates a response y=(y1,…,yT)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) token by token, where the state at step tt is st=(x,y<t)s_{t}=(x,y_{<t}) and the action is at=yt∼πθ(⋅∣st)a_{t}=y_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t}).

In the reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) setting [10, 31], a scalar reward is assigned only at the terminal step: rT=ℛ⁡(x,y)r_{T}=\mathcal{R}(x,y), rt=0r_{t}=0 for t<Tt<T. With discount factor γ=1\gamma=1, the return from any state equals the terminal reward: Gt=rT≜GG_{t}=r_{T}\triangleq G. The state-value function is Vπ​(s)=𝔼π​[G∣st=s]V^{\pi}(s)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G\mid s_{t}=s], and the observed return GG is a stochastic realization whose variance arises solely from the randomness of future actions under π\pi.

PPO and GRPO.

Both PPO [23] and GRPO [10, 25] optimize a clipped surrogate objective but differ in how they estimate advantages. Under RLVR conditions (γ=λ=1\gamma{=}\lambda{=}1, terminal-only reward), the PPO advantage reduces to (see Appendix A.2 for the full GAE derivation):

A^tPPO=G−V^ϕ​(st),\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{PPO}}=G-\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{t}), (1)

where V^ϕ\hat{V}_{\phi} is a learned critic providing a state-dependent baseline. GRPO eliminates the critic and instead computes a response-level advantage from batch statistics. Concretely, for each prompt xx, a batch of KK responses {y(i)}i=1K\{y^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{K} is sampled from the current policy, yielding returns {Gi}i=1K\{G_{i}\}_{i=1}^{K} with batch mean G¯ℬ=1K​∑i=1KGi\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}G_{i} and standard deviation σ⁡(Gℬ)\sigma(G_{\mathcal{B}}). The GRPO advantage is then:

A^iGRPO=Gi−G¯ℬσ⁡(Gℬ),\hat{A}_{i}^{\mathrm{GRPO}}=\frac{G_{i}-\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}}}{\sigma(G_{\mathcal{B}})}, (2)

where G¯ℬ\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}} and σ⁡(Gℬ)\sigma(G_{\mathcal{B}}) are the batch mean and standard deviation of returns, serving as a constant baseline shared across all tokens.

2.2 The Impact of Critic Quality on Policy Optimization

Returning to 𝒬1\mathcal{Q}_{1} (is the boundary observable?), we quantify critic quality via the explained variance (EV) metric, a standard indicator from regression analysis [24]:

ev=1−Var​(G−V^ϕ​(s))Var⁡(G),\mathrm{ev}=1-\frac{\mathrm{Var}(G-\hat{V}_{\phi}(s))}{\mathrm{Var}(G)}, (3)

which measures the fraction of return variance accounted for by the critic. Intuitively, ev>0\mathrm{ev}>0 indicates that the critic captures meaningful state-dependent signal, whereas ev≤0\mathrm{ev}\leq 0 means the critic’s estimation noise exceeds the signal it provides—its predictions are worse than a constant baseline.

Observation 1: A noisy critic hurts the actor.

We train a PPO policy on Sokoban and track the batch-level EV throughout training (see Appendix D.1 for details). As shown in Figure 2(a), EV remains consistently low during the first ∼150{\sim}150 training steps, indicating that the critic’s predictions are less accurate than a simple constant baseline during this phase. This poor critic quality has two visible consequences: gradient norms are notably elevated (Figure 2(b)), reflecting high-variance policy updates driven by noisy advantage estimates, and the training success rate remains low and unstable (Figure 2(c)), showing that the actor struggles to learn under unreliable critic guidance.

To further confirm the causal link between critic quality and actor performance, we conduct a controlled experiment: injecting Gaussian noise (σδ=0.3\sigma_{\delta}=0.3; the mean absolute state value is ≈0.5\approx 0.5) into a converged critic’s outputs. As shown in Figure 2(d), performance degrades monotonically as the noise level increases, with complete collapse at σ=10\sigma{=}10 where EV is driven far below zero. This confirms that negative EV is a reliable indicator of harmful critic influence, and that the relationship between critic quality and actor performance is not merely correlational but causal.

Observation 2: Reducing critic variance helps the actor.

We conduct two complementary interventions on the same Sokoban and FrozenLake setups (see Appendix D.2 for details): (i) Cold-start: replacing the critic’s output with the batch mean G¯ℬ\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}} during the first 50/25 steps, and (ii) Warm-up: pre-training the critic alone for 200 steps before the actor begins updating. Both interventions yield faster convergence and more stable training curves (Figure 3), confirming that suppressing critic variance during low-quality phases directly benefits the policy.

These observations suggest that the choice between a learned critic and a batch-mean baseline should not be fixed a priori, but should adapt to the critic’s current quality. In the following subsection, we formalize this intuition through a Kalman filtering lens.

2.3 A Kalman Filtering Perspective on Baseline Selection

To precisely locate the boundary (𝒬2\mathcal{Q}_{2}), we observe that choosing a baseline is fundamentally a state-estimation problem: both the critic V^ϕ​(s)\hat{V}_{\phi}(s) and the batch mean G¯ℬ\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}} are noisy estimates of the true value Vπ​(s)V^{\pi}(s), and the best baseline is the one with lower estimation error. This is exactly the setting addressed by the Kalman filter [14, 19], which optimally fuses two noisy estimates by weighting each inversely to its error variance.

Setup.

The observed return decomposes as G=Vπ​(s)+ϵG=V^{\pi}(s)+\epsilon with sampling noise R≜𝔼⁡[Var⁡(G∣s)]R\triangleq\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(G\mid s)]. The two competing baselines have distinct error structures: (i) the critic V^ϕ​(s)=Vπ​(s)+δ⁡(s)\hat{V}_{\phi}(s)=V^{\pi}(s)+\delta(s) with estimation error variance PA≜Var⁡(δ)P_{A}\triangleq\mathrm{Var}(\delta), and (ii) the batch mean G¯ℬ\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}} whose deviation from any specific state value has variance PB≜Vars​(Vπ​(s))P_{B}\triangleq\mathrm{Var}_{s}(V^{\pi}(s)). The minimum-variance linear combination of these two estimators assigns the critic a weight of 1−K∗1-K^{*} with the optimal gain K∗=PA/(PA+PB)K^{*}=P_{A}/(P_{A}+P_{B}) (see Appendix A.1 for the full derivation).

Connection to explained variance.

The EV metric (Eq. (3)) directly encodes the relative reliability of the two estimators. Substituting the variance decomposition into the definition of EV yields:

ev=PB−PAPB+R.\mathrm{ev}=\frac{P_{B}-P_{A}}{P_{B}+R}. (4)

Since the denominator PB+RP_{B}+R is always positive, the sign of EV is determined solely by PB−PAP_{B}-P_{A}. This means ev=0\mathrm{ev}=0 marks the exact boundary where PA=PBP_{A}=P_{B}, i.e., where the critic’s estimation noise equals the state signal it captures. Above this boundary (ev>0\mathrm{ev}>0), the critic outperforms the batch mean; below it (ev≤0\mathrm{ev}\leq 0), critic noise dominates. The sampling noise RR compresses the magnitude of EV but preserves its sign, keeping this boundary robust under high stochasticity.

3 Methodology

Building on the Kalman filtering framework of Section 2.3, we now formalize when a critic helps or hurts (Section 3.1), unify PPO and GRPO as two extremes of the Kalman gain (Section 3.2), and derive the EVPO algorithm (Section 3.3).

3.1 The Performance Collapse Boundary

From Eq. (4), the sign of EV is governed by PB−PAP_{B}-P_{A}. We formalize this as:

In words, the critic inflates advantage variance whenever its estimation noise (PAP_{A}) exceeds the state signal it captures (PBP_{B}), and ev=0\mathrm{ev}=0 is the exact tipping point. Since the sign of EV is computable from a single batch, this boundary is directly observable during training.

Computing EV from a training batch.

Replacing the population variances in Eq. (3) with sample variances over a batch of MM rollouts ℬ={(ym,Gm)}m=1M\mathcal{B}=\{(y_{m},G_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M} from the same prompt gives the batch-level EV:

ev^ℬ=1−Varℬ​(Gm−V^ϕ​(sm))Varℬ​(Gm),\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}}=1-\frac{\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{B}}(G_{m}-\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{m}))}{\mathrm{Var}_{\mathcal{B}}(G_{m})}, (6)

computed from the critic values already obtained for advantage estimation, with no additional forward passes.

3.2 PPO and GRPO as Kalman Extremes

Under RLVR conditions (γ=λ=1\gamma{=}\lambda{=}1, terminal-only reward), PPO and GRPO can be unified into the form A^t=G−b⁡(st)\hat{A}_{t}=G-b(s_{t}), differing only in the choice of baseline b⁡(st)b(s_{t}) (see Appendix A.2 for the detailed derivation). This difference maps directly onto the Kalman gain KK:

  • •

    PPO (critic mode, K=0K{=}0, full critic trust): b⁡(st)=V^ϕ​(st)b(s_{t})=\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{t}). The baseline is entirely model-driven; the Kalman filter places zero weight on the evidence-driven estimator.

  • •

    GRPO (batch-mean mode, K=1K{=}1, no critic trust): b⁡(st)=G¯ℬb(s_{t})=\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}}. (Since 1/σ⁡(Gℬ)1/\sigma(G_{\mathcal{B}}) does not affect the gradient direction.) The baseline is entirely evidence-driven; the critic is discarded and the batch mean serves as a constant baseline for all tokens.

In other words, PPO and GRPO are not fundamentally different algorithms but rather two extreme operating points of the same Kalman baseline-selection spectrum. PPO implicitly assumes PA≪PBP_{A}\ll P_{B} (the critic is always reliable), while GRPO implicitly assumes PA≫PBP_{A}\gg P_{B} (the critic is never worth using). Neither assumption holds uniformly across training, motivating an adaptive approach.

3.3 EVPO: Adaptive Baseline Selection via EV Gating

Having established where the collapse boundary lies (𝒬2\mathcal{Q}_{2}), we now turn to 𝒬3\mathcal{Q}_{3}: can this boundary be exploited online? The Kalman framework prescribes the optimal baseline as a continuous interpolation of the two estimators:

b⁡(s)=(1−K)​V^ϕ​(s)+K​G¯ℬ,K=PAPA+PB∈[0,1].b(s)=(1-K)\,\hat{V}_{\phi}(s)+K\,\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}},\quad K=\frac{P_{A}}{P_{A}+P_{B}}\in[0,1]. (7)

However, computing KK directly is infeasible: both PA=Var⁡(V^ϕ​(s)−Vπ​(s))P_{A}=\mathrm{Var}(\hat{V}_{\phi}(s)-V^{\pi}(s)) and PB=Vars​(Vπ​(s))P_{B}=\mathrm{Var}_{s}(V^{\pi}(s)) depend on the unknown true value Vπ​(s)V^{\pi}(s), making the continuous KK non-identifiable in practice. We therefore reduce the domain of KK to {0,1}\{0,1\}, corresponding to the two extremes: K=0K{=}0 (PPO, full critic trust) and K=1K{=}1 (GRPO, no critic). The decision boundary PAPA+PB=12\frac{P_{A}}{P_{A}+P_{B}}=\tfrac{1}{2} (i.e., PA=PBP_{A}=P_{B}) corresponds exactly to ev=0\mathrm{ev}=0 by Theorem 1. While the value of KK is non-identifiable, its position relative to 12\tfrac{1}{2} can be determined by the sign of ev^ℬ\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}} (Eq. (6)). This yields the EVPO switching rule:

b(st)={V^ϕ​(st),if ​ev^ℬ>0(K<12:trust critic),G¯ℬ,if ​ev^ℬ≤0(K≥12:retreat to batch mean),b(s_{t})=\begin{cases}\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{t}),&\text{if }\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}}>0\quad(K<\tfrac{1}{2}:\;\text{trust critic}),\\[4.0pt] \bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}},&\text{if }\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}}\leq 0\quad(K\geq\tfrac{1}{2}:\;\text{retreat to batch mean}),\end{cases} (8)

where ev^ℬ\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}} is the batch-level EV defined in Eq. (6).

Variance guarantee.

By construction, EVPO selects the lower-variance baseline at each step:

Var⁡(A^EVPO)=R+min⁡(PA,PB),\mathrm{Var}(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{EVPO}})=R+\min(P_{A},\;P_{B}), (9)

which is no greater than Var⁡(A^PPO)=R+PA\mathrm{Var}(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{PPO}})=R+P_{A} or Var⁡(A^GRPO)=R+PB\mathrm{Var}(\hat{A}^{\mathrm{GRPO}})=R+P_{B} at every training step. Over the course of training, this per-step guarantee accumulates: EVPO avoids the critic’s noisy cold-start phase (PA≫PBP_{A}\gg P_{B}) while fully exploiting a mature critic (PA≪PBP_{A}\ll P_{B}).

4 Experiments

Our experiments aim to validate that the per-step variance reduction of EVPO (Eq. 9) translates into consistent performance gains over fixed baselines (Section 4.2). We further analyze whether EV serves as a reliable indicator of the PAP_{A}-vs-PBP_{B} balance throughout training (Section 4.3) and whether the theoretically derived collapse boundary ev=0\mathrm{ev}=0 (Theorem 1) coincides with the empirically optimal switching threshold (Section 4.4).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Evaluation.

We evaluate on four tasks that span diverse agent interaction paradigms. Sokoban [13] and FrozenLake [5] are multi-turn grid-world games requiring sequential planning under sparse rewards, with FrozenLake additionally introducing environmental stochasticity. WebShop [34] is an interactive web-based agentic task involving multi-step instruction following and decision making. MATH targets competition-level mathematical reasoning trained and evaluated on problems in DAPO-Math-17k [35].

Baseline.

We compare EVPO against the Base LLM without RL post-training, two critic-based methods (PPO [23] and StarPO-S [31]), and two critic-free methods (GRPO [25] and DAPO [35]). For the Math task we use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct [21] as the base model; the other three tasks use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct [21]. To ensure fair comparison, the hyperparameter recipe is tuned independently per task but kept consistent across all methods on the same task. Full configurations are provided in Appendix B.

4.2 Main Results

The stronger fixed baseline varies across tasks: critic-based methods (PPO, StarPO-S) clearly outperform critic-free methods (GRPO, DAPO) on Sokoban, FrozenLake, and WebShop, while critic-free methods are more competitive on MATH. EVPO surpasses both families in every case (Table 1), confirming that it is not tied to a single favorable regime but adapts to the task-specific PAP_{A}-vs-PBP_{B} balance.

As shown in Figure 4, EVPO leads or matches the strongest baseline at most training stages across all four tasks. This indicates that adaptive switching takes effect continuously—not by recovering from a poor start or catching up late, but by maintaining lower-variance advantage estimates throughout the optimization trajectory. The per-step variance guarantee (Eq. 9) predicts exactly this behavior: since EVPO selects the lower-variance baseline at every step, its cumulative benefit should manifest as a sustained advantage rather than a late-stage correction.

4.3 Gating Behavior Analysis

Figure 5 tracks the critic-selection probability over training. Across Sokoban, WebShop, and MATH, the batch-mean mode is triggered frequently in early training and progressively less as training continues, consistent with the expectation that PAP_{A} decreases as the critic improves. A notable exception is FrozenLake, where gating frequency reverses around step 80, coinciding with training stagnation (Figure 4(b)). This suggests that when the policy enters a difficult region, critic quality can temporarily regress, and the adaptive gating responds by retreating to the batch-mean baseline.

4.4 EV Threshold Sensitivity

We vary the switching threshold across {−0.2,−0.1,0,0.1,0.2}\{-0.2,-0.1,0,0.1,0.2\} while keeping all other configurations fixed. As shown in Figure 6(a, c, e, g), the theoretically derived boundary ev=0\mathrm{ev}=0 (Theorem 1) is not merely a theoretical convenience but the practically optimal operating point. The training landscape in Figure 6(b, d, f, h) reveals an asymmetry in the two deviation directions. A positive threshold under-utilizes the critic: training progresses normally in early stages but collapses later when policy refinement requires state-dependent advantage estimates that the batch mean cannot provide. A negative threshold over-utilizes the critic: the immature critic’s noise slows early training, and in later stages, unreliable value predictions on certain state subsets continue to inject variance. These two failure modes reveal that, as we argued theoretically, the zero threshold is precisely the boundary separating the PA>PBP_{A}>P_{B} and PA<PBP_{A}<P_{B} regimes.

5 Related Work

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for LLMs.

RL-based LLM post-training has evolved from actor-critic architectures such as PPO [23], which rely on a learned value function for variance reduction via GAE [22], toward critic-free alternatives that bypass the value network entirely. GRPO [25, 10, 30] replaces the learned baseline with intra-group reward normalization and has become the dominant paradigm; REINFORCE++ [11] further stabilizes this family via global batch normalization, and similar estimators like RLOO [1] and DAPO [35] further demonstrate that a critic is often dispensable for single-turn, verifiable tasks.

Yet critic-free methods face two systematic challenges: group-relative advantages introduce statistical bias, systematically underestimating hard prompts and overestimating easy ones [12, 16], and uniform trajectory-level credit assignment degrades severely in long-horizon settings lacking early termination [4, 7], compelling multi-turn frameworks such as RAGEN [31] to reintroduce the critic for stable training. All existing approaches resolve this tension between critic-free simplicity and critic-based credit assignment [15] through a static, a priori architectural commitment that either always uses or always discards the critic, regardless of its current predictive quality.

Adaptive Baselines and Explained Variance.

Reducing policy-gradient variance without detrimental bias is a foundational RL challenge [32, 28]. State-dependent baselines are theoretically unbiased but rely on the assumption that the value network is accurate; in LLM post-training, the vast state space and sparse rewards frequently violate this assumption, causing the baseline subtraction to inject more noise than it removes. Prior work addresses this through two complementary strategies: redesigning the baseline structure itself [2], or using critic quality as a signal to adapt hyperparameters such as λ\lambda in GAE [17] or to filter uninformative transitions [9].

However, these methods treat critic quality as a signal to tune hyperparameters or curate data while preserving the actor-critic architecture. EVPO departs from both strategies by elevating EV from a passive diagnostic to a architecture selection criterion that determines whether the critic is used at all, switching to critic-free estimation when the value network becomes mathematically harmful.

6 Conclusion

We presented EVPO, an adaptive RL method for LLM post-training that uses explained variance to switch between critic-based and batch-mean advantage estimation at each training step. By casting baseline selection as a Kalman filtering problem, we proved that the sign of EV is the exact boundary separating the variance-reducing from the variance-inflating critic regime (Theorem 1), and that EVPO’s per-step switching yields advantage variance no greater than the better of PPO and GRPO at every step.

Across four tasks spanning multi-turn planning, agentic interaction, and mathematical reasoning, EVPO consistently outperforms both fixed baselines, regardless of which one is stronger on a given task. The gating analysis confirms that EVPO’s adaptation tracks critic maturation over training, and the threshold sensitivity study validates that the theoretically derived zero boundary is empirically optimal.

Limitations

Population vs. batch EV.

Theorem 1 characterizes the collapse boundary in terms of population EV, whereas EVPO switches on batch EV computed from finite samples. We do not provide finite-sample concentration bounds for the switching rule, though the threshold sensitivity analysis (Section 4.4) suggests that zero is a robust practical threshold.

Resource overhead.

EVPO maintains a critic network throughout training, including iterations where the batch-mean mode is selected, and therefore retains the memory footprint of PPO rather than matching fully critic-free methods.

Task coverage.

Our evaluation spans four tasks across three domains. Tasks with dense intermediate rewards, learned reward models, or substantially different rollout lengths may exhibit different EV dynamics.

Appendix A Extended Proofs and Derivations

Detailed proofs and derivations are provided in this appendix.

A.1 Detailed Kalman Filtering Analogy

We provide here the full state estimation analogy and derivation that motivates the EV-based switching criterion introduced in Section 2.3.

State estimation analogy.

We cast baseline construction as a scalar state estimation problem. The hidden state to be estimated is the true value function x=Vπ​(s)x=V^{\pi}(s). For each sample in a training batch, the observed return decomposes as

G=Vπ​(s)+ϵ,ϵ∼(0,R),R≜𝔼⁡[Var⁡(G∣s)],G=V^{\pi}(s)+\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim(0,R),\quad R\triangleq\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{Var}(G\mid s)], (10)

where RR is the irreducible sampling noise arising from the stochasticity of future actions under π\pi. Two competing estimators of Vπ​(s)V^{\pi}(s) are available at each training step:

  • •

    Model-driven prediction (Critic). x^A=V^ϕ​(s)=Vπ​(s)+δ⁡(s)\hat{x}_{A}=\hat{V}_{\phi}(s)=V^{\pi}(s)+\delta(s), where δ⁡(s)\delta(s) denotes the critic’s estimation error with variance PA≜Var⁡(δ)P_{A}\triangleq\mathrm{Var}(\delta). This parallels the state prediction in a Kalman filter: it exploits learned state features but carries modelling noise whose magnitude depends on the critic’s current training quality.

  • •

    Evidence-driven observation (Batch mean). x^B=G¯ℬ\hat{x}_{B}=\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}}, the empirical mean return over the batch, which approximates 𝔼​[Vπ​(s)]\mathbb{E}[V^{\pi}(s)]. Its error relative to any specific state ss has variance PB≜Vars​(Vπ​(s))P_{B}\triangleq\mathrm{Var}_{s}(V^{\pi}(s)), paralleling the observation noise in a Kalman filter: it reflects how much true state values vary within the batch, and is large when the batch covers heterogeneous states.

The sampling noise RR affects both estimators symmetrically and controls the sensitivity of the EV diagnostic without altering its sign.

Optimal fusion and the Kalman gain.

The Kalman filter combines the two estimators via a linear combination b⁡(s)=(1−K)​x^A+K​x^Bb(s)=(1-K)\,\hat{x}_{A}+K\,\hat{x}_{B} that minimizes the mean squared error 𝔼⁡[(b⁡(s)−Vπ​(s))2]\mathbb{E}[(b(s)-V^{\pi}(s))^{2}]. The optimal Kalman gain is:

K∗=PAPA+PB.K^{*}=\frac{P_{A}}{P_{A}+P_{B}}. (11)

When K∗<12K^{*}<\tfrac{1}{2} (i.e., PA<PBP_{A}<P_{B}), the critic is more reliable than the batch mean and should receive higher weight; when K∗≥12K^{*}\geq\tfrac{1}{2} (i.e., PA≥PBP_{A}\geq P_{B}), the critic’s estimation noise dominates the state signal it provides, and the baseline should retreat toward the batch mean.

Connection to explained variance.

Substituting the variance decompositions from Eq. (10) into the definition of EV yields:

ev=PB−PAPB+R.\mathrm{ev}=\frac{P_{B}-P_{A}}{P_{B}+R}. (12)

Since the denominator is always positive, the sign of EV is determined solely by PB−PAP_{B}-P_{A}:

  • •

    ev>0⟺PA<PB⟺K∗<12\mathrm{ev}>0\;\Longleftrightarrow\;P_{A}<P_{B}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;K^{*}<\tfrac{1}{2}: the critic outperforms the batch mean, corresponding to the regime where PPO’s state-dependent baseline is advantageous;

  • •

    ev≤0⟺PA≥PB⟺K∗≥12\mathrm{ev}\leq 0\;\Longleftrightarrow\;P_{A}\geq P_{B}\;\Longleftrightarrow\;K^{*}\geq\tfrac{1}{2}: the critic’s noise exceeds its signal, corresponding to the regime where GRPO’s constant baseline is preferable.

A.2 GAE Derivation under RLVR Conditions

Proximal Policy Optimization [23] estimates advantages via Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) [22]:

A^tGAE=∑l=0T−1−t(γ​λ)l​δt+l,δt=rt+γ​V^ϕ​(st+1)−V^ϕ​(st),\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{GAE}}=\sum_{l=0}^{T-1-t}(\gamma\lambda)^{l}\delta_{t+l},\quad\delta_{t}=r_{t}+\gamma\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{t+1})-\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{t}), (13)

where V^ϕ\hat{V}_{\phi} is a learned critic and λ∈[0,1]\lambda\in[0,1] controls the bias–variance trade-off. The policy is updated by maximizing a clipped surrogate objective that constrains the ratio πθ​(at|st)/πθold​(at|st)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}|s_{t})/\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_{t}|s_{t}).

Under RLVR conditions (γ=λ=1\gamma=\lambda=1, terminal-only reward rT=ℛ⁡(x,y)r_{T}=\mathcal{R}(x,y), rt=0r_{t}=0 for t<Tt<T), GAE reduces to:

A^tPPO=∑l=tT−1(rl+V^ϕ​(sl+1)−V^ϕ​(sl))=G−V^ϕ​(st),\hat{A}_{t}^{\mathrm{PPO}}=\sum_{l=t}^{T-1}\bigl(r_{l}+\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{l+1})-\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{l})\bigr)=G-\hat{V}_{\phi}(s_{t}), (14)

where the telescoping sum cancels all intermediate critic terms (with the terminal state value defined as 0), leaving the advantage as the deviation of the observed return from the critic’s state-dependent prediction.

Appendix B Tasks

We evaluate on four tasks spanning multi-turn grid-world control, interactive web agents, and single-turn mathematical reasoning. All training code is based on the RAGEN2 framework [31], which wraps verl for PPO-style LLM post-training and provides multi-turn agent environments.

Sokoban.

We use the CoordSokoban variant of the RAGEN2 Sokoban environment [13]. Each episode instantiates a 6×66\times 6 grid with one box and one target, procedurally generated from an environment seed. The observation at each step is a symbol grid together with zero-indexed coordinates of the player, the box, and the target. The action space is {Up,Down,Left,Right}\{\textsc{Up},\textsc{Down},\textsc{Left},\textsc{Right}\}; the policy is prompted to emit an action sequence of length up to two per turn, separated by “||” and enclosed in <answer>…</answer> tags. A trajectory consists of up to 1010 executed actions across up to 55 turns. The reward is terminal and binary: +1+1 if all boxes end on targets, 00 otherwise, with an additional format penalty of −0.1-0.1 for malformed outputs.

FrozenLake.

We use the CoordFrozenLake variant wrapping the Gymnasium FrozenLake-v1 environment [5]. The map is a 4×44\times 4 grid with randomly placed holes, the start tile, and the goal tile; the map layout is resampled per environment seed. Transitions are stochastic (is_slippery=True): the commanded action succeeds with probability 1/31/3, and with probability 2/32/3 the agent slips perpendicular to the intended direction. The observation is again a symbol grid plus coordinates of start, goal, player, and all holes. The action space is {Left,Down,Right,Up}\{\textsc{Left},\textsc{Down},\textsc{Right},\textsc{Up}\}, with up to 1010 actions per trajectory across up to 55 turns. The reward is terminal and binary: +1+1 if the player reaches the goal, 00 if the player falls into a hole or exhausts the action budget; a format penalty of −0.1-0.1 is applied for malformed outputs.

WebShop.

WebShop [34] is an interactive web-navigation task in which the agent must locate and purchase a product matching a natural-language instruction. We use the webshop-minimal fork with the small product catalogue shipped with RAGEN2. At each turn the agent observes the current page (search box, product list, or product detail) together with the list of clickable elements, and produces exactly one action drawn from search[keywords] or click[element], again wrapped in <answer>…</answer>. A trajectory consists of up to 99 actions across up to 99 turns. The reward is the built-in WebShop matching score in [0,1][0,1], delivered only at the terminal click[buy now].

MATH.

We use DAPO-Math-17k [35] (17,267 competition-level problems) for both training and validation: the full training set is used for RL updates, and a fixed subset of 32 problems, held out from training, is used for evaluation. Each problem is a single-turn reasoning task (max_turn=1): the policy is prompted with the problem statement and must emit a <think>…</think> block followed by the final numerical answer inside <answer>…</answer>. The reward is terminal and binary: +1+1 if the final answer matches the ground truth (after normalization), 00 otherwise.

Appendix C Baselines and Hyperparameters

We compare EVPO against a Base-LLM reference and four RL baselines that span both critic-based and critic-free families.

  • •

    Base LLM. Instruction-tuned Qwen2.5 without any RL post-training, prompted zero-shot with the same task template as the RL runs.

  • •

    PPO [23]. Standard clipped-surrogate PPO with GAE advantages. Under our RLVR setting (γ=λ=1\gamma{=}\lambda{=}1, terminal-only reward) this reduces to the PPO advantage of Eq. (1) with a learned, state-dependent critic.

  • •

    StarPO-S [31]. A multi-turn PPO variant introduced by RAGEN that filters the lowest-variance rollouts before each update (rollout_filter_ratio=0.25=0.25, rollout_filter_metric==reward_variance) to stabilize long-horizon agentic training.

  • •

    GRPO [25]. Critic-free; the baseline is the response-level batch mean, normalized by the batch standard deviation.

  • •

    DAPO [35]. A modern critic-free variant built on GRPO with (i) dynamic sampling that discards groups whose rewards are all identical and resamples up to max_num_gen_batches=5\texttt{max\_num\_gen\_batches}{=}5 times until enough informative groups are collected; (ii) clip-higher asymmetry (εlow,εhigh)=(0.2,0.28)(\varepsilon_{\text{low}},\varepsilon_{\text{high}})=(0.2,0.28); (iii) token-level loss aggregation (loss_agg_mode==token-mean); and (iv) no std normalization of advantages and no in-reward KL term.

All five methods (PPO, StarPO-S, GRPO, DAPO, EVPO) share the same rollout stack, tokenizer, and environment code, and differ only in the advantage estimator and the listed hyperparameters. EVPO itself uses PPO-style training (critic and actor with clipped surrogate) and only changes the baseline subtracted from the return, as prescribed by the EV-gating rule (Eq. (8)).

Table 2 lists the hyperparameters that differ across methods or tasks. Learning rates are tuned per task on the Base-LLM vs. PPO gap on a single seed and then kept identical across methods on the same task for fair comparison, except where a differing value is itself a defining feature of the algorithm (see the caption of Table 2).

Appendix D Details of the Preliminary Experiments

This section gives the exact protocols for the two preliminary studies that motivate EVPO in Section 2.

D.1 PPO on Sokoban: EV, Gradient Norm, Success Rate (Figure 2)

We train a PPO agent on Sokoban using the same setting as the Sokoban PPO main experiment (Sokoban PPO row of Table 2). At every step we record, over the same batch of M=16×8=128M=16\times 8=128 rollouts used for the update: (i) the batch-level EV ev^ℬ\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}} defined in Eq. (6); (ii) the pre-clipping gradient norm of the actor; (iii) the training success rate (fraction of rollouts with terminal reward =1=1). Shaded regions in Figure 2(a–c) highlight the first ≈150\approx 150 steps where ev^ℬ\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}} remains near or below 00.

Noise-injection experiment (Figure 2(d)).

We first train a PPO agent on FrozenLake to convergence under the same hyperparameters as the FrozenLake row of Table 2 for 200200 steps, then continue training with i.i.d. Gaussian noise added to every critic output: V^ϕ​(s)↦V^ϕ​(s)+ξ\hat{V}_{\phi}(s)\mapsto\hat{V}_{\phi}(s)+\xi with ξ∼𝒩⁡(0,σδ2)\xi\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{\delta}^{2}). We sweep σδ∈{0.3, 1, 3, 10}\sigma_{\delta}\in\{0.3,\,1,\,3,\,10\}, corresponding to noise magnitudes from well below to well above the mean absolute state value (≈0.5\approx 0.5). Each noise level is run for an additional 150150 training steps, starting from the same converged checkpoint. We report the smoothed validation success rate; Fig. 2(d) shows monotone degradation with complete collapse at σδ=10\sigma_{\delta}{=}10, precisely the regime where ev^ℬ\widehat{\mathrm{ev}}_{\mathcal{B}} is driven far below zero.

D.2 Cold-start and Critic Warmup (Figure 3)

We run two interventions on top of the Sokoban and FrozenLake PPO setups.

Cold-start.

During the first KcoldK_{\text{cold}} training steps we replace every critic output in the advantage computation by the batch mean, A^tcold-start=G−G¯ℬ\hat{A}_{t}^{\text{cold-start}}=G-\bar{G}_{\mathcal{B}}; after step KcoldK_{\text{cold}} we resume standard PPO with the original critic. We set Kcold=50K_{\text{cold}}=50 on Sokoban and Kcold=25K_{\text{cold}}=25 on FrozenLake, chosen to cover the EV-negative phase of Fig. 2(a). The critic itself is always trained with its usual MSE loss so that by step KcoldK_{\text{cold}} it has had time to warm up.

Critic warmup.

Before the actor receives any gradient, we train the critic alone for Kwarm=200K_{\text{warm}}=200 steps using the same rollouts as full PPO but with ∇θℒactor\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\text{actor}} set to zero. After step KwarmK_{\text{warm}} we switch on actor updates and continue with standard PPO.

In both interventions all other hyperparameters match the PPO rows of Table 2. Figure 3 compares each intervention against the unmodified PPO baseline under the same seed and hardware; the consistent improvements confirm that it is specifically the suppression of critic-driven variance (rather than any secondary effect of the interventions) that benefits the policy.
